memory_verse: "The Kingdom of God is righteousness and peace and joy in the Holy Spirit." —Romans 14:17, NASB
sermon_title: The Danger of Pretending to Be Righteous

days.focus: The Danger of Becoming Immune to God's Word
days.message_recap: The sermon opened with the illustration of a train horn that passes by unheard despite its loudness, warning that just as familiarity can make us immune to that sound, years of hearing God's word can make us immune to its conviction. The speaker then turned to Matthew 23:27 to introduce the week's central danger: pretending to be righteous — looking beautiful on the outside like a whitewashed tomb while being full of death on the inside.
days.message_quote: Week after week we hear it and God maybe wants to say something to us and just like that train going by every night and I don't know that it even went there like that week after week God's word when it's spoken to us can go by pass by.
days.verse_reflection: Romans 14:17 says the kingdom of God is 'righteousness and peace and joy in the Holy Spirit' — not in performance, not in reputation, not in religious routine. Romans 8:9 warns plainly that if the Spirit of God does not actually dwell in us and govern us, we do not belong to Christ at all. This cuts through every external appearance. Sit honestly before God today: is the righteousness you carry through the week the kind that flows from the Holy Spirit living inside you, or is it a tone of voice, a Sunday manner, a cultivated impression that you carefully maintain in front of others? The train of God's word has been going past — has it actually struck you like the hammer Jeremiah describes, or have you grown so familiar with it that it no longer reaches the inner man at all?
days.daily_prayer: Lord, I confess that I have heard Your word so many times that it has sometimes passed me by like a train in the night — loud, but leaving me undisturbed. I ask You to make Your word strike me today like a hammer, reaching past my outer conduct and penetrating what I am truly like in secret. Let the righteousness and peace and joy that belongs to Your kingdom be real in me by Your Spirit, not a performance I maintain in front of others.

days.focus: Judas: How a Genuine Disciple Slipped into Pretending
days.message_recap: The sermon called believers away from having different 'versions' of themselves in different settings, and then focused on Judas Iscariot as a case study — arguing that he began as a genuinely wholehearted disciple, chosen from among many, and entrusted with the money box, yet gradually began pilfering from it while building a public reputation for caring about the poor. The speaker used John 12:3-6 to show how Judas's outward concern for the poor masked an inward reality of theft and self-interest.
days.message_quote: Now he said this not because he was concerned about the poor people but because he was a thief and as he had the money box he used to pilfer what was put into it.
days.verse_reflection: The memory verse places righteousness, peace, and joy together — and 1 John 1:6-7 makes clear that walking in the light is the only condition under which genuine fellowship with God and with other believers is even possible. Judas walked alongside Jesus in broad daylight while conducting a hidden life in darkness, and the two lives never collided in repentance — only in ruin. The question 1 John presses on us is not whether we use the right language about the light, but whether our actual daily walk — our private financial choices, our private speech, the things we do when no one who knows us is present — is genuinely in the light. Is there anything you are currently doing that you know you would stop immediately if the people who respect you could see it? That gap between the private and the public life is precisely where pretending begins.
days.daily_prayer: Father, I am convicted that the distance between my public reputation and my private conduct can grow quietly, just as it did in Judas, without my even marking the moment it began. I ask You to shine Your light on any area of my life where I am managing an impression rather than living in the truth. Make the righteousness of Your kingdom real in me from the inside out, by Your Holy Spirit, not by what others see of me.

days.focus: Reputation, Correction, and the Moment That Reveals the Heart
days.message_recap: The sermon examined how thoroughly Judas had built his reputation — so completely that even when Jesus directly identified the betrayer at the Last Supper, the other disciples still did not suspect him and assumed he was going out to give to the poor. The speaker then traced a turning point: when Jesus corrected Judas ('Leave her alone') over the anointing at Bethany, Judas immediately went to the chief priests to arrange the betrayal, revealing that a man's response to correction exposes whether his inner life matches his outer reputation.
days.message_quote: And I see this is a danger, a great danger. If you turn with me to Matthew 26 again, why was it so difficult to see this deception in this man?
days.verse_reflection: Romans 14:17 describes the kingdom of God as righteousness, peace, and joy in the Holy Spirit — and Hebrews 12:5-6 shows us the path by which that peace and joy actually become durable: through receiving the Father's discipline rather than resenting it. A person who is truly walking in the Spirit will receive correction as a gift — even when it stings, even when it comes in front of others, even when it touches a carefully protected reputation. The question Hebrews presses on us is not whether we can tolerate gentle encouragement, but whether we can receive a sharp and public correction without becoming cold toward the one who gave it. Consider honestly: is there a correction you received — from a pastor, a spouse, a friend, a passage of Scripture — that you are still quietly nursing a grievance over, rather than having genuinely received it and repented?
days.daily_prayer: Lord, I confess that my first instinct when I am corrected is often to defend myself, to remember the correction and forget every grace You have shown me through the same person. I ask You to give me a heart that receives Your discipline as a son receives it from a father who loves him — openly, humbly, and without self-justification. Let Your peace rule in me not because life is smooth, but because I am walking honestly before You.

days.focus: Small Hidden Sins, Forgotten Mercies, and the Certainty of Being Found Out
days.message_recap: The sermon argued that Judas's downfall was partly rooted in forgetting all the specific, personal kindnesses Jesus had shown him — the times Jesus chose him, rested with him, and even promised him a throne — while fixating on a single moment of correction. The speaker also traced how repeated, uncaught sin progressively hardens the conscience, using Ecclesiastes 8:11 and Numbers 32:23 to warn that sin which is not judged immediately only emboldens further sin, and that what is not set right here will follow a person to the judgment seat.
days.message_quote: Because of this sentence against the evil deed is not executed quickly. That means soon as he stole the first time he didn't get caught. The hearts of the son of man are fully given to evil.
days.verse_reflection: Romans 14:17 says the kingdom of God is righteousness — not merely the forgiveness of past sin, but actual present righteousness lived out. Romans 6:16 confronts us with a stark reality: every time we yield to a sin, we are actively presenting ourselves as its slave, and that slavery deepens with each repeated act of yielding. The sermon illustrated this with Judas's pilfering — what began with a single act of taking grew, through repeated yielding, into a pattern so entrenched that even three and a half years with Jesus did not reverse it. The question Romans 6 puts to us is not whether we regret a sin in the moment after we commit it, but whether we are genuinely presenting ourselves to God as instruments of righteousness — in the specific area where our conscience has already spoken to us. What is the sin your conscience has named, that you have overridden more than once, telling yourself it is too small to address?
days.daily_prayer: Father, I acknowledge that every time I have overridden my conscience and repeated a sin I already knew was wrong, I was making myself more its slave and less Yours. I do not want to be the person who arrives at judgment with sins that followed me there because I never dealt with them here. By Your Holy Spirit, give me the courage to judge myself honestly today — to name the thing, bring it into the light, and set it right while there is still time.

days.focus: The Stone Must Be Removed — God Wants Living Bones, Not Hidden Ones
days.message_recap: The sermon used the raising of Lazarus in John 11 as a picture of what God wants to do for every believer who has been hiding dead men's bones behind a beautiful tombstone: Jesus commands the stone to be removed and calls us to come out, promising that the stench we fear will be replaced by the glory of God. The speaker then turned to Ezekiel 37 to show that dry bones brought out into the open can become a mighty army when God breathes His Spirit into them.
days.message_quote: If you believe, you'll see the glory. And that's what happened to Lazarus. He didn't come out with stench. That wasn't the message of his life. The message of the life, he was dead and he's now alive.
days.verse_reflection: The memory verse declares that the kingdom of God is joy in the Holy Spirit — but Romans 8:13 tells us the condition on which the Spirit's life actually flows: 'if by the Spirit you are putting to death the deeds of the body, you will live.' The joy is real, but it is inseparable from a willingness to let the Spirit expose and mortify the hidden things. Martha's fear in John 11 — 'Lord, by this time there will be a stench' — is exactly the fear that keeps believers locked in their tombs: the fear that what comes out when the stone is removed will be worse than the death of staying hidden. But Romans 8:13 frames this differently — the Spirit is not the source of shame when things come into the light; He is the power by which the deeds of the body are actually put to death and replaced with life. What is the 'stone' you are afraid to let Jesus remove, and are you willing today to trust that what He brings to light, He also has power to transform?
days.daily_prayer: Lord Jesus, I confess that I have been more afraid of the stench that might come out than I have been willing to trust Your promise that those who believe will see Your glory. I ask You now to remove whatever stone I have rolled in front of the hidden parts of my life, and to call me out by name, just as You called Lazarus. Fill me with Your Holy Spirit so that the dry bones become something alive and useful to You.

days.focus: Receiving Correction Like Peter, Not Like Judas — and Coming Out of the Grave
days.message_recap: The sermon closed by contrasting Peter and Judas: Peter was corrected repeatedly — by Jesus, by the Father at the Transfiguration, and publicly by Paul in Galatia — yet each time he received it and was not destroyed by it, and this capacity to receive correction is presented as the reason he endured to the end. Judas, by contrast, was corrected far less harshly but could not receive it, and the speaker called every listener to come out of their grave today, warning that those who come out when Jesus calls will rise to the resurrection of the righteous.
days.message_quote: He found a man that he knew that if he corrected Peter that he would receive it. He won't talk back. He won't justify it. He won't give an excuse. He would accept it quietly and repent of it.
days.verse_reflection: Romans 14:17 ends with the phrase 'in the Holy Spirit' — righteousness, peace, and joy are not achievements of willpower or religious discipline; they are the fruit of a life genuinely governed by the Spirit. Galatians 5:22-25 names these qualities as fruit, meaning they grow from a living root, not from human effort at appearing righteous. Paul closes that passage with the demand that if we live by the Spirit we must also 'keep in step with the Spirit' — a phrase that implies active, ongoing surrender to His leading in specific moments, not a general agreement with correct theology. Peter kept in step by receiving each correction and moving forward; Judas broke step the moment correction threatened his reputation and stopped walking with the Spirit altogether. The honest question for today, at the end of this week, is this: where in your life are you still walking by the flesh — by what manages your reputation, by what feels safe, by what others are unlikely to notice — rather than by the Spirit who is actually present inside you and who knows everything?
days.daily_prayer: Heavenly Father, I come to the end of this week and I ask You to make me the kind of person who can be corrected — by Your word, by Your Spirit, by godly people around me — without becoming bitter or cold. I do not want to be someone who looked good on the outside for years and then was found empty; I want to walk with You in the Spirit every single day, bearing the genuine fruit of righteousness and peace and joy that only You can produce. Remove the stone, Lord — whatever is still hidden — and call me out into the life You have promised.
